title: Federation, One Word Apart
blurb: Seven identity and access minimal pairs — the vocabulary CISSP loves to swap on federation, SSO and MFA questions.
source: Chapple CISSP SG 10ed ch.13-14 · April-2024 outline 5.2, 5.3, 5.4

pairs.dimension: proving who you are vs what you're allowed to do

a.text: A help-desk agent enters a one-time code from her phone after her password to confirm she really is the account holder.
a.why: Verifying the claimed identity against credentials — knowledge, ownership, or characteristic — happens before any access decision is made.

b.text: Once the same agent is logged in, the system checks her role and lets her view billing records but blocks her from deleting accounts.
b.why: This step decides what an already-verified identity may do — a separate check that happens only after authentication has succeeded.

pairs.dimension: vouching for who the subject is vs handing over a scoped slice of her data

a.text: When a research fellow opens the genomics portal, her university's identity system sends the portal a signed XML statement that this session belongs to a verified faculty member.
a.why: A signed XML assertion vouching for who the subject is, passed to the site that must decide whether to admit her, is this protocol's core job.

b.text: When the same fellow opens the genomics portal, her university's identity system instead issues the portal a token good only for reading her stored sequence files, and her university password never leaves the university.
b.why: Handing a relying site a narrow, revocable slice of access to one resource, without disclosing the owner's credential or stating who she is, is what this framework grants.

pairs.dimension: an access token alone vs an added token that also asserts who the user is

a.text: A nurse connects the shift-swap app to her hospital account, and the hospital returns one token: it lets the app read and add entries on her rota, and carries nothing about who she is.
a.why: A token that only authorizes actions on a resource, silent on the resource owner's identity, is this framework's whole scope — access, never authentication.

b.text: The same nurse connects the same app to the same hospital account, and alongside that rota token the hospital returns a second, signed token naming her and attesting that it authenticated her just now.
b.why: The extra signed identity token, layered on the same delegated-access exchange so the app learns who signed in rather than merely what it may do, is this layer's addition.

pairs.dimension: one org's resources vs multiple orgs' trust relationship

a.text: An employee logs into the corporate directory once each morning and reaches the intranet, the ticketing tool, and the file share, all inside the same company.
a.why: One authentication event unlocking multiple resources within a single organization's own access control system is the narrower case.

b.text: That same employee later uses her employer's login to access a training platform run by an entirely separate company that has agreed to trust her employer's identity assertions.
b.why: Crossing an organizational boundary on the strength of a pre-established trust relationship between separate entities is what turns single sign-on into this broader arrangement.

pairs.dimension: holds the identity vs consumes the assertion

a.text: In a SAML exchange, the third party that stores the user's credentials and issues the signed assertion confirming who logged in is this entity.
a.why: Owning the identity store and producing the authentication assertion, rather than the resource the user wants, is this side's role.

b.text: The travel-booking application that receives that signed assertion and, trusting it, lets the user in without collecting a password of its own is this entity.
b.why: Relying on someone else's assertion to grant access to its own resource, rather than holding the identity itself, is the defining trait of the other half of the pair.

pairs.dimension: counts toward multifactor vs describes a policy engine's input

a.text: A login requires a password plus a hardware token's generated code — two different proof categories, knowledge and ownership, combined before access is granted.
a.why: A distinct category of identity proof, drawn from knowledge, ownership, or characteristic, that must differ in kind from any other factor already used, is what strengthens authentication here.

b.text: A policy engine evaluates the requester's department, the sensitivity label on the file, and the time of day before deciding whether the already-authenticated user may open it.
b.why: Characteristics about the subject, resource, or environment that feed an access-control policy after identity is already established belong to authorization, not to strengthening the login itself.

pairs.dimension: provisions accounts automatically on first login vs requires an admin to create them in advance

a.text: A contractor's first federated login to the design portal is accepted and the portal builds her local account from the assertion on the spot, no ticket having been filed beforehand.
a.why: Building the local account from the assertion the moment the first federated login arrives, with no prior administrative step, is what just-in-time provisioning adds on top of federation.

b.text: The same contractor's first federated login to the design portal is refused until an administrator has created her local account there in advance from a filed ticket.
b.why: Requiring the local account to exist before any federated assertion will be honored is the baseline arrangement that just-in-time provisioning was built to remove.
